explain.title: Ungrouped and grouped data
explain.body: Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data. When the same data is arranged into groups or classes, it is called grouped data.

explain.title: Frequency distribution
explain.body: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. The frequency tells how many data values fall in each class.

explain.title: Making class intervals
explain.body: First find the range by subtracting the smallest value from the greatest value. Divide the range by the desired number of classes to find the class size, then form the class limits and count the data with tally marks.

explain.title: Unequal class widths
explain.body: When the class widths are unequal, adjust each rectangle height by dividing its class frequency by its class width. These proportional heights are also called adjusted frequencies.

explain.title: Midpoints and frequency polygons
explain.body: A frequency polygon is a line graph of a frequency distribution in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints. Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits.

mistakes: Using the range formula in the wrong order: subtract the smallest value from the greatest value.
Starting the class intervals at a value other than the smallest data value when following the textbook method.
Counting a value twice or missing it while making tally marks.
Using the original frequencies as histogram heights when class widths are unequal; divide each frequency by its class width.
Using class limits instead of midpoints for the horizontal values of a frequency polygon.
Forgetting to label axes, state a scale, or join the polygon points with straight lines.

explain.title: What is central tendency?
explain.body: The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set. It gives one representative value for a whole set of data.

explain.title: Arithmetic mean
explain.body: It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations. For ungrouped data, use x̄ = Σx/n. For grouped data, use x̄ = Σfx/Σf, where x is the midpoint of each class.

explain.title: Median
explain.body: Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. For grouped data, find cumulative frequencies, locate the n/2-th item and use Median = ℓ + (h/f)(n/2 − c).

explain.title: Mode and weighted mean
explain.body: In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. When observations have different weights, use weighted mean: x̄w = ΣWX/ΣW.

mistakes: Finding a median without arranging ungrouped observations first.
For an even number of values, choosing one middle value instead of averaging the two middle values.
Using class limits instead of class midpoints when finding a grouped arithmetic mean.
For a grouped median, using the wrong cumulative frequency: c is the cumulative frequency before the median class.
For grouped mode, mixing up f1 (the preceding frequency) and f2 (the following frequency).
For weighted mean, dividing by the number of values instead of by the sum of the weights.
Leaving out units or rounding before completing the calculation.

explain.title: Frequency and frequency distributions
explain.body: Frequency is the number of times a value occurs. A frequency distribution organises data into values or classes and records their frequencies.

explain.title: Histograms and frequency polygons
explain.body: A histogram displays frequencies with adjoining rectangles. To make a frequency polygon, plot frequencies at class midpoints and join the points; it can also be drawn on a histogram.

explain.title: Class boundaries and midpoints
explain.body: For integer class limits, class boundaries make neighbouring intervals join. The midpoint, or class mark, is the average of the two class limits.

explain.title: Mean and weighted mean
explain.body: The mean is the sum of observations divided by their number. For a frequency distribution, use Σfx ÷ Σf; for weighted data, the weights determine how much each value contributes.

explain.title: Median, mode and range
explain.body: Arrange data to find the median: choose the middle value, or average the two middle values. The mode occurs most often. The range is the greatest value minus the smallest value.

notes.title: Making and reading frequency distributions
notes.answer: A frequency distribution organises data into classes and shows the frequency of each class.
notes.explanation: Ungrouped data is raw information that has not been arranged into classes. A frequency distribution groups the data and shows how many values fall in each class. For unequal class widths, use adjusted frequency (frequency divided by class width) for the histogram height.
notes.simple: Put the data into groups, count how many values are in each group, and show the counts in a table or graph.
examples: For the class 10–14, the midpoint is (10 + 14)/2 = 12.
If a class has frequency 18 and width 3, its adjusted frequency is 18/3 = 6.
steps: Find the range: greatest value − smallest value.
Find the class size: range ÷ number of classes, then round as shown in your textbook.
Make the class limits and use tally marks to count the data.
Write the number of tallies as the frequency.
For unequal class widths, find adjusted frequency by dividing frequency by class width.
For a frequency polygon, plot each class frequency against its midpoint and join the points with straight lines.
notes.checkQuestion: A class has frequency 24 and width 4. What is its adjusted frequency?

notes.title: Measures of Location: Mean, Median and Mode
notes.answer: The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their number. Median is the middle value in arranged data, mode is the most frequent value, and weighted mean accounts for different weights.
notes.explanation: A measure of central tendency gives one representative value for a data set. Use the arithmetic mean when you need the average, the median when you need the middle value, the mode when you need the most frequent value, and the weighted mean when observations have different importance.
notes.simple: These measures describe a data set with one useful number: its average, middle, most common value, or weighted average.
examples: For 2, 5, 7, the median is 5 because it is the middle value after arranging the data.
steps: For an arithmetic mean, add the values and divide by their number.
For grouped data, use x̄ = Σfx/Σf, where x is the class midpoint.
For a median, arrange ungrouped data first; for grouped data, locate the median class using n/2 in the cumulative frequencies.
For a mode, identify the most frequent value, or use the grouped-data mode formula.
For a weighted mean, use x̄w = ΣWX/ΣW.

notes.title: Information Handling: Review
notes.explanation: Information handling helps us organise data and describe it using tables, graphs and averages. A frequency table shows how often values occur. A histogram and frequency polygon display grouped data. Mean, median and mode describe the centre of a data set.
notes.simple: Organise the data, then use a graph or an average to describe it.
examples: For 3, 5, 5, 7, the mode is 5 because it occurs most often.
steps: For a frequency table, count how many times each value or class occurs.
For grouped data, use class boundaries for a histogram and class midpoints for a frequency polygon.
Mean = sum of the values ÷ number of values. For a frequency table, use Σfx ÷ Σf.
To find the median, arrange the data in order and find the middle value or the average of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that occurs most often; the range is the greatest value minus the smallest value.
